p.src: Pilgrim reported, “Master, that place is neither a prince’s mansion nor the home of some wealthy lord; it looks like a convent, Taoist abbey, or monastery. We shall know the truth when we reach it.” Hearing this, Tripitaka whipped his horse onward. Master and disciples arrived before the gate and saw a stone tablet set above it, bearing the three characters “Yellow Flower Abbey.” Tripitaka dismounted. Bajie said, “Yellow Flower Abbey is a Taoist establishment. We may as well go in and meet its occupants. Though their dress differs from ours, our religious cultivation is the same.” Sha Monk said, “That is true. For one thing, we can go in and admire the scenery; for another, we can unload the baggage and let the animals rest. If circumstances permit, we can arrange some vegetarian food for Master.”

p.src: The elder agreed, and all four entered together. On the second gate they saw a pair of spring couplets: “Yellow shoots and white snow fill the immortals’ abode; Jade herbs and jeweled flowers grace the Taoist’s home.” Pilgrim laughed. “This is one of those Taoists who burn thatch and refine elixirs, tend their furnaces, and carry their pots about.” Tripitaka pinched him and said, “Guard your tongue, guard your tongue. We neither know him nor claim kinship with him. We shall be here only briefly, so why concern ourselves with what he does?” Before he had finished, they passed through the second gate. p.src: Seeing him, Tripitaka called loudly, “Venerable Immortal, this poor monk offers his greetings.” The Taoist jerked up his head and started at the sight of them. Dropping the medicine in his hand, he secured his hairpin, straightened his robes, and descended the steps to welcome them. “Venerable Master, forgive me for failing to greet you sooner. Please come inside and sit.” Delighted, the elder ascended the hall. When the door was pushed open, they saw sacred images of the Three Pure Ones, with an incense burner and incense on the altar table. He immediately took incense, placed it in the burner, and made three circuits of reverence before exchanging courtesies with the Taoist. Then he went to the guest seats and sat down with his disciples. The Taoist hastily called the acolytes to prepare tea. Two young acolytes promptly went inside to find a tea tray, wash the cups, wipe the spoons, and prepare tea and fruit. Their frantic bustle soon alerted those old enemies.

p.src: It turned out that the seven female fiends of Webbed Hollow had studied under the same master as this Taoist. After putting on their old clothes and calling out their sons, they had come straight here. They were cutting out clothes in the rear quarters when they suddenly saw an acolyte preparing tea, and asked, “Boy, what guests have arrived to make you so busy?” The acolyte replied, “Four Buddhist monks arrived just now, and Master told us to prepare tea.” A fiend asked, “Is there a fair-faced, plump monk among them?” “Yes,” he replied. She asked again, “Is there one with a long snout and great ears?” “Yes,” he replied. The fiend said, “Quickly serve the tea, then signal your master to come in. I have something urgent to tell him.” Sure enough, the acolyte carried out five cups of tea. The Taoist drew his robes together and offered one cup to Tripitaka with both hands, then served Bajie, Sha Monk, and Pilgrim. When they had finished their tea, the cups were collected. The boy gave him a signal, and the Taoist rose slightly, saying, “Please remain seated, gentlemen.” He instructed, “Boy, set down the tea tray and attend our guests. I shall return shortly.” For the moment, the elder and his disciples, accompanied by one acolyte, went outside the hall to look around; of this we shall say no more.

p.src: We now tell how the Taoist entered the abbot’s quarters. The seven women all fell to their knees and cried, “Elder brother, elder brother, hear what your little sisters have to say!” The Taoist helped them up, saying, “When you arrived this morning, you wanted to tell me something. But as it happened, I was making pills today, and this batch must not be seen by women, so I did not answer you. Now I have guests outside as well. Whatever you have to say can wait.” The fiends said, “Elder brother, we must report that this very matter concerns the arrival of those guests, which is why we dare tell you now; if they leave, there will be no use speaking of it.” The Taoist laughed. “Listen to yourselves, worthy sisters! How can it be that you must speak precisely because guests have arrived? Have you gone mad? Even if I were not one who quietly cultivates immortality, but an ordinary householder with wife, children, and domestic affairs, I would still wait until the guests had gone before attending to them. How can you be so inconsiderate as to make me put on a false front? Let me go back outside.” The fiends all seized him again, saying, “Elder brother, calm your anger. Let us ask you: where did those guests in front come from?” The Taoist scowled and gave no answer. The fiends said, “When the boy came in just now to fetch the tea, we heard him say they were four Buddhist monks.” Feigning anger, the Taoist said, “What of it if they are monks?” The fiends said, “Among those four monks, is there one fair-faced and plump, and another with a long snout and great ears? Did you ask where they came from?” The Taoist said, “Those two are indeed among them, but how do you know? I suppose you have seen them somewhere before?”

p.src: The women said, “Elder brother, you do not know the circumstances behind this. That monk was sent by the Tang court to fetch scriptures from the Western Heaven. He came to our cave this morning to beg a vegetarian meal. We sisters had heard of the Tang Monk’s fame, so we seized him. The Taoist asked, “Why did you seize him?” The women replied, “We had long heard it said that the Tang Monk possesses the true body of one who has cultivated himself through ten incarnations, and that anyone who eats a piece of his flesh will gain longevity and immortality. That is why we seized him. Later, that long-snouted, big-eared monk trapped us in the Cleansing Spring. First he stole our clothes; then he displayed his powers and insolently insisted on bathing with us, and we could not stop him. He leapt into the water and changed into a catfish, wriggling back and forth between our legs in an attempt to molest and deceive us. He was utterly shameless. Then he jumped out of the water and resumed his true form. When he saw that we would not submit, he wielded a nine-pronged rake and tried to take our lives. Had we not possessed some skill, we would nearly have died by his vicious hand; thus we escaped for our lives, trembling with fear. We also sent your foolish nephews to fight him, but we do not know whether they are alive or dead. We have come especially to seek refuge with you, elder brother, hoping that for the sake of our old fellowship as fellow students, you will avenge our wrongs today.” On hearing this, the Taoist became angry. His expression and tone changed as he said, “So these monks are truly this rude and shameless! Set your minds at ease. I shall deal with them.” The women thanked him, saying, “If you strike at them, elder brother, we shall all help you fight.” The Taoist said, “There is no need to fight, no need to fight. As the saying goes, ‘Once blows are exchanged, one’s standing falls by three parts.’ All of you, follow me.”

p.src: The Daoist said to the seven women, “Sisters, if an ordinary mortal takes this treasure of mine, a mere one li will kill him as soon as it enters his belly; even an immortal needs only three li to be killed. These monks may possess some cultivation, so we must use three li on each of them. Quickly, fetch the scales.” One of the women hurriedly brought a small balance and said, “Weigh out one fen and two li, and divide it into four portions.” They then took twelve red dates, split them slightly, and stuffed one li of poison into each set before dividing them among four teacups. They put two black dates into another teacup, set all five upon a tray, and the Daoist said to the women, “Let me go and question them. If they are not from the Tang realm, that will be the end of it; but if they have come from the Tang, I shall order fresh tea, and you must have the boy carry this tea out. Once they drink it, every one of them will die. Thus I shall avenge you and put an end to your distress.” The seven women were endlessly grateful.

p.src: The Daoist changed his robe, assumed a courteous and humble manner, and went out. He invited the Tang Monk and his disciples back to their seats in the reception room and said, “Reverend Master, please do not take offense. I went to the rear just now to instruct my young disciples to gather some greens and radishes and prepare a vegetarian meal for you. That is why I left you unattended.” Tripitaka said, “This poor monk has come to pay his respects empty-handed. How could I dare trouble you to bestow a meal on us?” The Daoist smiled. “You and I are both men who have left the household. The moment one enters a religious gate, one is entitled to three sheng of provisions. How can you call yourself empty-handed? May I ask from what holy mountain you come, Reverend Master? And what brings you here?” Tripitaka replied, “This poor monk was sent by the sovereign of the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to fetch scriptures from the Great Thunderclap Monastery in the Western Heaven. We happened to pass your immortal abode just now and came in to pay our respects with all sincerity.” Hearing this, the Daoist’s face blossomed with delight. “Reverend Master, you are a Buddha of loyal heart and great virtue. This humble Daoist did not know and failed to welcome you from afar. Forgive me, forgive me.” He called, “Boy, quickly bring fresh tea, and make haste with the meal as well.” The young attendant went inside, and the women beckoned him over, saying, “Here is fine tea already prepared. Carry it out.” Sure enough, the boy carried out the five cups of tea. The Daoist hurriedly took one of the cups containing red dates in both hands and offered it to the Tang Monk. Seeing Bajie’s great bulk, he took him for the senior disciple; he took Monk Sha for the second disciple; and seeing that Pilgrim was small in stature, he took him for the third disciple. Thus it was only the fourth cup that he offered to Pilgrim.

p.src: Sharp-eyed Pilgrim accepted the cup and had already noticed that the cup remaining on the tray contained two black dates. He said, “Sir, let you and me exchange cups.” The Daoist smiled. “To tell you the truth, Elder, I am a poor Daoist in these wild mountains and had neither tea nor fruit ready. Just now I searched for fruit myself in the back, but found only these twelve red dates, enough to make four cups of tea in your honor. Yet I could not accompany you with an empty cup, so I used two inferior dates to make this cup for myself. This is merely an expression of my humble respect.” Pilgrim laughed. “What are you saying? The ancients said, ‘At home, no man is truly poor; poverty on the road can kill a man.’ You have a settled home, so how can you call yourself poor? It is traveling monks like us who are truly poor. Let us exchange cups. Let us exchange.” Hearing this, Tripitaka said, “Wukong, this Immortal Elder truly means to honor his guests. Drink it. Why exchange cups?” Pilgrim had no choice. He held the cup in his left hand, covered it with his right, and watched the others.

p.src: Now Bajie was hungry as well as thirsty, and his appetite was enormous. Seeing three red dates in his cup, he raised it and gulped everything straight into his belly. Their master drank his tea, and Monk Sha drank his too. In a moment, Bajie’s face changed color, tears streamed from Monk Sha’s eyes, and froth issued from the Tang Monk’s mouth. Unable to remain seated, all three collapsed unconscious upon the floor.

p.src: The Great Sage knew at once that it was poison. He raised his teacup and hurled it straight at the Daoist’s face. The Daoist shielded himself with his sleeve. With a clang, the cup fell and shattered to pieces. The Daoist said angrily, “You monk are utterly coarse and boorish! Why did you smash my cup?” Pilgrim cursed him. “You beast! Look at what has happened to my three companions! What grievance have I with you, that you should use poisoned tea to drug my people senseless?” The Daoist said, “You ignorant beast have brought disaster upon yourself. Do you truly not know it?” Pilgrim replied, “We have only just entered your gate. We had barely taken our seats and spoken of where we came from, without exchanging so much as a harsh word. What disaster could we possibly have caused?” The Daoist asked, “Did you beg a meal at the Cave of Silken Web? Did you bathe in the Spring of Cleansing Filth?” Pilgrim said, “The ones at the Spring of Cleansing Filth were seven female fiends. Since you have mentioned this, you must be in league with them and must surely be a fiend yourself. Do not run! Take this blow from my staff!” What a Great Sage! From his ear he drew the gold-banded cudgel, gave it a shake until it was as thick as a rice bowl, and struck straight at the Daoist’s face. The Daoist hastily turned aside and dodged the blow, then drew a precious sword to meet him.

p.src: As the two traded curses and blows, they soon alarmed the female fiends inside. All seven rushed out together, crying, “Senior Brother, do not trouble yourself. Let your little sisters capture him.” At the sight of them, Pilgrim grew even more furious. Wielding his iron staff in both hands, he unleashed all his techniques and charged among them, striking wildly. The seven bared their bosoms and thrust out their snow-white bellies, working magic from their navels. Ropes of silk came bubbling out in wild profusion, forming a canopy that covered Pilgrim beneath it. Seeing that matters had gone awry, Pilgrim turned over, recited a spell, and sprang into a somersault. With a crash he burst through the canopy and escaped. Suppressing his temper, he hovered sullenly in the air and looked down. The fiends’ silken cords gleamed and crossed in countless strands like warp and weft racing through a loom. In an instant, the towers, terraces, halls, and pavilions of Yellow Flower Abbey were completely hidden from sight. Pilgrim said, “Formidable, truly formidable! Luckily I did not fall into their hands. No wonder Zhu Bajie suffered so many falls. What am I to do against the likes of this? My master and junior brother have also been poisoned. This band of fiends are united in purpose and heart, yet I do not know their origins. I had better go and question the local earth god.”

p.src: The Great Sage descended from his cloud, made the magic sign, and uttered the true-word spell “Om,” summoning the old local god once more. Trembling, the god knelt by the roadside, kowtowed, and said, “Great Sage, you went to rescue your master. Why have you come back?” Pilgrim said, “I rescued my master this morning, and before we had gone far we came upon a Yellow Flower Abbey. p.src: Pilgrim went outside the Yellow Flower Abbey, plucked seventy hairs from his tail, breathed immortal breath upon them, and cried, “Change!” At once they changed into seventy little Pilgrims. Then he breathed immortal breath upon the gold-banded cudgel and cried, “Change!” It immediately changed into seventy-one forked cudgels with two prongs. He gave each little Pilgrim one and wielded one himself. Standing outside, they twisted the silken cords around their forks, then all heaved together to a shouted rhythm and snapped every cord, each winding up more than ten catties of silk. Seven spiders were dragged out from within, each with a body as large as a bushel basket. Each drew in its legs, tucked down its head, and cried only, “Spare us! Spare us!” The seventy little Pilgrims held down the seven spiders and refused to release them. Pilgrim said, “Do not beat them yet. Make them return my master and junior brothers to me.” The monsters shrieked, “Elder Brother, give him back the Tang Monk and save our lives!” The Daoist ran out from inside and said, “Sisters, I mean to eat the Tang Monk. I cannot save you.” Pilgrim flew into a rage at this and said, “Since you will not return my master, just watch what happens to your sisters.” The Great Sage shook the forked cudgel, restoring it to a single iron staff, raised it in both hands, and mercilessly smashed all seven spider spirits to pulp.

p.src: Pilgrim was thrown into confusion. He could only spin about within the golden radiance: he could take no step forward and could not move his feet backward, as though turning inside a barrel. Helpless and unable to contain his impatience, he made one desperate leap upward. He broke through the golden light, but fell headfirst with a thud and felt pain shoot through his head. He quickly reached up and felt his head; the skin over his crown had been battered soft. In distress he thought, “What rotten luck! What rotten luck! Even this head of mine has failed me today. Ordinarily neither blades nor axes can harm it, so how has this golden light battered its flesh soft? Before long it is sure to fester. Even if it heals, I shall still get lockjaw from the wound.” After a while, unable to endure his frustration, he reasoned with himself again: “I cannot go forward, backward, left, or right, and I cannot break out above. What am I to do? To hell with it—I will go down!”

p.src: Just as the Handsome Monkey King was overcome with grief, he suddenly heard someone weeping behind the mountain. He straightened himself, wiped away his tears, and turned to look. He saw a woman dressed in full mourning. In her left hand she carried a bowl of cold rice gruel, and in her right several sheets of yellow spirit money to burn. She came from that direction, taking a step with every sob. Pilgrim nodded and sighed, “Indeed, ‘Tearful eyes meet tearful eyes; one broken heart encounters another.’ I wonder what has made this woman weep. Let me ask her.” Before long the woman came forward and met Pilgrim. Pilgrim bowed and asked, “Good lady, for whom are you weeping?” Holding back her tears, the woman said, “My husband quarreled with the abbot of the Yellow Flower Abbey over the purchase of bamboo poles, and the abbot killed him with poisoned tea. I have brought this bundle of spirit money to burn, to honor the bond between husband and wife.” Hearing this, Pilgrim's eyes filled with tears. When the woman saw this, she grew angry and said, “How senseless you are! I grieve and sorrow for my husband, yet why do you put on tearful eyes and a woeful face to mock and deceive me?”

p.src: Pilgrim bowed and said, “Lady Bodhisattva, please calm your anger. I am Sun Wukong the Pilgrim, chief disciple of Tang Sanzang, the imperial younger brother commissioned by the Great Tang in the Eastern Land. On our journey to the Western Heaven, we passed Yellow Flower Abbey and stopped there to rest our horse. The Daoist in that abbey—I do not know what sort of fiend he is—had sworn brotherhood with seven spider spirits. The spider spirits tried to murder my master in Webbed Hollow, but my fellow disciples Bajie and Sha Monk and I rescued him. The spider spirits fled to the Daoist, twisted right and wrong, and accused us of intending to deceive them. The Daoist felled my master and my two fellow disciples with poisoned tea; all three men and the horse are trapped in his abbey. I alone had not drunk his tea. I smashed the cup, and he began fighting me. Amid the uproar, the seven spider spirits ran out and spewed silken cords that entangled me, but I escaped by magic. I questioned the local earth god, who told me the creature’s true form. Then I used my body-division magic to tear the silken cords apart, dragged the fiends out, and beat them to death with my staff. The Daoist then sought revenge for them, raising his precious sword to fight me. After sixty bouts he was defeated. He stripped off his clothes, revealed a thousand eyes beneath his ribs, and shot forth ten thousand golden rays that pinned me fast. Unable either to advance or retreat, I finally changed into a pangolin scale and bored my way out underground. While I was grieving bitterly, I suddenly heard you weeping, and so I asked what troubled you. When I saw you repaying your husband with this paper money, I thought that, should my master perish, I would have nothing at all with which to repay him. I lamented my own plight and fell into sorrow—how would I dare mock you?”

p.src: The woman set down the food, water, and paper money, then apologized to Pilgrim: “Forgive me, forgive me. I did not know that you too were in distress. From what you have just told me, it is clear that you do not know that Daoist. He is actually the Hundred-Eyed Demon Lord, also called the Many-Eyed Fiend. Since you command such transformations, escaped the golden rays, and fought him for so long, you must possess tremendous powers; nevertheless, you still cannot approach that wretch. I shall tell you of a holy immortal whom you may invite. She can break the golden rays and subdue the Daoist.” Hearing this, Pilgrim hastily bowed and said, “Since you know his origins, Lady Bodhisattva, please instruct me. Tell me who that holy immortal is, and I shall go beg for help. By rescuing my master, I shall also avenge your husband.” The woman said, “I shall tell you, and you may invite her to subdue the Daoist; but that may only avenge us, for I fear your master cannot be saved.” Pilgrim asked, “Why can he not be saved?” The woman replied, “That wretch’s poison is exceedingly virulent. Within three days of being poisoned, a person’s very marrow rots away. I fear you will return too late, and that is why he cannot be saved.” Pilgrim said, “I travel swiftly. However far it may be, I need only half a day.” The woman said, “Since you travel swiftly, listen carefully: it is a thousand li from here to that place. There stands a mountain called Purple Cloud Mountain. Within it lies Thousand Flowers Cave, home to a holy immortal named Bodhisattva Pilanpo, who can subdue this fiend.” Pilgrim asked, “In what direction does that mountain lie? Which way must I go?” Pointing with her hand, the woman said, “Go due south, and you will reach it.” When Pilgrim turned his head to look, the woman had already vanished. Pilgrim hurriedly bowed and cried, “Which Bodhisattva are you? My wits were muddled after burrowing underground, and I failed to recognize you. I beg you to leave your name so that I may thank you.” A voice called from midair, “Great Sage, it is I.” Pilgrim hastily looked up and saw that it was the Venerable Mother of Mount Li. He caught up with her in the sky and thanked her, saying, “Venerable Mother, what brings you here to instruct me?” The Venerable Mother said, “I have just returned from the Dragon Flower Assembly. Seeing your master in peril, I disguised myself as a mourning widow and used the pretext of my husband’s death to save him from dying. Go quickly and invite her, but do not say that I directed you. That holy immortal is rather apt to take offense at others.”

p.src: Unable to restrain his steps, Pilgrim approached and called, “Bodhisattva Pilanpo, my greetings.” The Bodhisattva immediately descended from the couch, joined her palms, and returned his greeting. “Great Sage, forgive me for not coming to welcome you. Where have you come from?” Pilgrim asked, “How did you recognize me as the Great Sage at once?” Pilanpo replied, “When you caused havoc in Heaven long ago, your likeness was circulated throughout the world. Who has not heard of you, and who would fail to recognize you?” Pilgrim said, “Indeed, ‘Good news stays at home, while bad news travels a thousand li.’ But now that I have reformed and entered the Buddhist fold, you know nothing of it?” Pilanpo asked, “When did you reform? Congratulations, congratulations.” Pilgrim said, “Only recently did I escape with my life and undertake to protect my master, the Tang Monk, on his journey west for the scriptures. At Yellow Flower Abbey, my master encountered a Daoist who felled him with poisoned tea. I fought the wretch, but he enveloped me in golden rays. I escaped only by exercising my divine powers. I heard that you could extinguish his golden rays, Bodhisattva, and have come expressly to beg your aid.” The Bodhisattva asked, “Who told you that? Since attending the Ullambana Assembly, I have not left my home for over three hundred years. I concealed my name and identity, and no one knows of me. How then did you learn?” Pilgrim replied, “I am a well-informed imp who can ferret out anything, wherever it may be.” Pilanpo said, “Very well, very well. I ordinarily would not go, but since the Great Sage has deigned to visit me, I cannot extinguish the virtuous endeavor of seeking the scriptures. I shall go with you.”

p.src: Pilgrim thanked her and said, “In my great ignorance, I have taken the liberty of pressing you. But may I ask what weapon you have brought?” The Bodhisattva replied, “I have an embroidery needle that can overcome the wretch.” Pilgrim could not help saying, “The Venerable Mother has misled me! Had I known it was an embroidery needle, there would have been no need to trouble you. Old Sun could have supplied a whole shoulder-load if asked.” Pilanpo said, “Your embroidery needles would be no more than steel or golden needles and would be of no use. This treasure of mine is neither steel, iron, nor gold. It was refined within the sun-eye of my son.” Pilgrim asked, “Who is your honored son?” Pilanpo replied, “My son is the Star Lord of the Pleiades.” Pilgrim was astonished beyond measure. Soon he saw the brilliant blaze of golden light in the distance. Turning to Pilanpo, he said, “Where the golden light shines is Yellow Flower Abbey.” Pilanpo took an embroidery needle from inside her collar. It was as thick as an eyebrow and five or six fen long. Holding it between her fingers, she tossed it into the air. A moment later there came a crack, and the golden rays were shattered. Pilgrim cried joyfully, “Bodhisattva, marvelous, marvelous! Find the needle! Find the needle!” Pilanpo held it out upon her palm and said, “Is this not it?” Pilgrim descended from the clouds with her and entered the abbey. There they saw the Daoist with his eyes closed, unable to take a step. Pilgrim cursed him: “You insolent fiend, pretending to be blind!” He drew the staff from his ear and was about to strike. Pilanpo caught hold of him and said, “Do not strike, Great Sage. First go and see your master.”

p.src: Wukong went straight to the guest quarters at the rear and found all three of them lying on the floor, frothing and spitting. Wukong wept and said, “What am I to do? What am I to do?” Bodhisattva Pilanpo said, “Great Sage, do not grieve. Since I have ventured out today, I may as well perform a hidden act of merit. I have antidote pills here. I shall give you three.” Wukong turned and bowed as he begged for them. The Bodhisattva took a torn paper packet from her sleeve, drew out three little red pills, and handed them to Wukong, telling him to put them into the sufferers’ mouths. Wukong pried open their jaws and pushed one pill into each mouth. Presently the medicine reached their stomachs, and all three began retching together. Once they had vomited up the poison, their lives were saved. Bajie was the first to scramble up, crying, “I was suffocating to death!” Tripitaka and Friar Sand also awoke, saying, “How terribly dizzy we are!” Wukong said, “There was poison in the tea you drank. It was Bodhisattva Pilanpo who saved you. Come and thank her at once.” Tripitaka raised himself, straightened his robes, and offered his thanks.

u.src: Wukong went straight to the guest quarters at the rear and found all three of them lying on the floor, frothing and spitting.
Wukong wept and said, “What am I to do?
What am I to do?”
Bodhisattva Pilanpo said, “Great Sage, do not grieve.
Since I have ventured out today, I may as well perform a hidden act of merit.
I have antidote pills here. I shall give you three.”
Wukong turned and bowed as he begged for them.
The Bodhisattva took a torn paper packet from her sleeve, drew out three little red pills, and handed them to Wukong, telling him to put them into the sufferers’ mouths.
Wukong pried open their jaws and pushed one pill into each mouth.
Presently the medicine reached their stomachs, and all three began retching together. Once they had vomited up the poison, their lives were saved.
Bajie was the first to scramble up, crying, “I was suffocating to death!”
Tripitaka and Friar Sand also awoke, saying, “How terribly dizzy we are!”
Wukong said, “There was poison in the tea you drank.
It was Bodhisattva Pilanpo who saved you. Come and thank her at once.”
Tripitaka raised himself, straightened his robes, and offered his thanks.

p.src: Bajie said, “Brother, where is that Daoist? Let me ask him why he tried to harm us like this!” Wukong recounted the whole affair concerning the spider spirits. Bajie snarled fiercely, “Since that scoundrel calls the spiders his sisters, he must be a monster too.” Pointing, Wukong said, “He is standing outside the hall, pretending to be blind.” Bajie raised his rake to strike, but Pilanpo stopped him, saying, “Marshal of the Heavenly Reeds, restrain your anger. The Great Sage knows that there is no one in my cave. Let me take him back to guard its gate.” Wukong said, “We are deeply grateful for your great kindness; how could we refuse? Only make him reveal his true form, so that we may see it.” Pilanpo said, “That is easily done.” She stepped forward and pointed a finger. The Daoist toppled into the dust and revealed his original form: a huge centipede spirit some seven feet long. Pilanpo hooked him up with her little finger, mounted an auspicious cloud, and returned directly to Thousand Flowers Cave.

p.src: Bajie leaned back in astonishment and said, “That old dame is formidable indeed! How did she subdue such a vicious creature so easily?” Wukong laughed. “I asked what weapon she had that could break his golden light. She said she possessed a little embroidery needle, forged by her son within the eye of the sun. When I asked who her honored son was, she said he was the Star Lord of the Pleiades. Now, the Pleiades Star is a cock, so this old dame must surely be a hen. Chickens are the greatest bane of centipedes; that is why she could subdue him.”

p.src: Hearing this, Tripitaka bowed again and again in reverence. Then he said, “Disciples, pack up and let us be on our way.” Friar Sand found some rice and grain inside, prepared a vegetarian meal, and they all ate their fill. They led out the horse, shouldered the baggage, and invited their master to leave. Wukong set a fire in the kitchen, and in an instant the entire abbey was burned to ashes. Then they strode away on their long journey. Indeed:
